questions.question: 1. The array 5, 4, 1, 2, 3 is sorted in ascending order. Which option provides the correctly sorted array?

answers.d: Depends on which data structure is used

explanations.a: Correct. Ascending order arranges the existing elements from smallest to largest: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This arrangement places the larger values before the smaller values.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This option duplicates elements that were not duplicated in the original array.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The required sorted order is determined by the values, not by the data structure used.

questions.question: 2. Which of the following statements about logarithms is correct?

explanations.b: Incorrect. These logarithms use different bases and do not have the same value.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The numerical comparison stated here is not correct.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The two logarithms have different numerical values.

questions.question: 3. Which of the following is true about binary trees?

answers.a: Every binary tree is either complete or full
answers.b: Every complete binary tree is also a full binary tree
answers.c: Every full binary tree is also a complete binary tree
answers.d: A perfect binary tree is both complete and full

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary trees can be neither complete nor full.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Completeness and fullness are different structural properties; a complete tree can contain a node with only one child.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A full tree does not necessarily have all levels filled from left to right.
explanations.d: Correct. A perfect binary tree has every internal node with two children and all levels completely filled, so it is both complete and full.

questions.question: 4. Level of a node is distance from root to that node. For example, level of root is 1 and levels of left and right children of root is 2. The maximum number of nodes on level $i$ of a binary tree is:

explanations.a: Correct. At level 1 there can be $2^0=1$ node, at level 2 there can be $2^1=2$ nodes, and in general the maximum is $2^{i-1}$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. With this formula, level 1 would contain 2 nodes, which is impossible because the root is the only node at level 1.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This formula gives more nodes than a binary tree can have at the stated level.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This expression does not follow the doubling pattern of the maximum number of nodes at successive levels.

questions.question: 5. What is the main purpose of arranging elements into a heap before performing Heap Sort?

answers.b: To establish the heap property so the required extreme element can be selected efficiently
answers.c: To preserve the original order of all elements
answers.d: To convert the array into a linked list

explanations.a: Incorrect. Heap construction changes the arrangement of elements but does not make their values equal.
explanations.b: Correct. The heap property places either the largest or smallest element at the root, depending on the heap type, supporting efficient selection during Heap Sort.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Heap construction is not intended to preserve the original ordering of elements.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Heap construction operates on an array representation and does not convert it into a linked list.

questions.question: 6. In a max-heap, which element is located at the root?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A max-heap orders each parent relative to its children in the opposite direction from this description.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The heap property does not require the root to be the median.
explanations.c: Correct. In a max-heap, every parent is greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum element is at the root.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The root is constrained by the heap property and is not arbitrary.

questions.question: 7. Which statement best describes the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up method?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Building a heap requires processing multiple nodes, so it cannot be completed in constant time for arbitrary $n$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. $O(\log n)$ describes the height of a heap and some individual heap operations, not the complete bottom-up construction.
explanations.c: Correct. Bottom-up heap construction runs in $O(n)$ time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. $O(n\log n)$ is a looser bound associated with repeated logarithmic-time insertions, not the optimal bottom-up construction.

questions.question: 8. During Heap Sort using a max-heap, what happens after the maximum element is moved to the end of the unsorted portion?

answers.a: The heap size is reduced and the remaining heap is restored
answers.b: The entire array is reversed immediately
answers.c: All elements are inserted into a second array
answers.d: The maximum element is moved back to the root

explanations.a: Correct. The placed maximum is excluded from the heap, and the remaining heap is restored so the next maximum can be selected.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Heap Sort does not require reversing the entire array after each extraction.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Standard in-place Heap Sort does not require copying all elements into a second array at this step.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The extracted maximum is kept in its final position rather than being moved back into the active heap.

questions.question: 9. What is the worst-case time complexity of Heap Sort for an array of $n$ elements?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Heap Sort performs more than a linear number of comparisons and heap adjustments in the worst case.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The heap structure limits the height of each adjustment, so the worst case does not require quadratic time.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sorting all $n$ elements requires substantially more work than a single logarithmic-time heap operation.
explanations.d: Correct. Building the heap takes $O(n)$ with bottom-up construction, followed by $n$ removals or adjustments costing $O(\log n)$ each, giving $O(n\log n)$ overall.
